pour-over-at-home.title: Brew a pour-over at home in four minutes
pour-over-at-home.excerpt: A glass dripper, a kettle and fifteen grams of coffee: the method we use behind the counter, slowed down.
content: Most of what makes a good cup happens before the water goes in. This is the method we teach at the counter, the one that works with our house blend and with the roaster's pick. It takes four minutes, five if you stop to smell it.
A dripper and a paper filter
A kettle, ideally with a thin spout
15 g of coffee, ground like sea salt
250 g of water just off the boil, about 94 °C
Scales, or a steady hand and a tablespoon
Rinse the paper filter with hot water. It warms the dripper and the cup, and takes away the papery taste. Pour that water away.
Weigh 15 g of coffee into the filter and give it a shake so the bed is flat. A flat bed means the water passes through evenly.

Pour about 40 g of water, just enough to wet all the grounds, and wait thirty seconds. Fresh coffee puffs up and bubbles as it lets go of gas; that is the bloom, and it is why freshly roasted beans matter.
If it does not bloom, the coffee is old. No method will fix that.
Pour in small circles from the middle outwards, up to 150 g.
Wait for the level to drop by a finger's width.
Let it drain. The whole brew should take three to four minutes.
Sour or thin? Grind finer next time. Bitter or dry? Grind coarser. Change one thing at a time and you will have your perfect cup within a week.

this-months-beans.title: Where this month's beans come from
this-months-beans.excerpt: Our roaster's pick is a washed coffee from Guji, in southern Ethiopia, from a washing station we have bought from for three years.
content: This month's roaster's pick comes from Guji, in the highlands of southern Ethiopia, where coffee grows wild under the forest canopy and smallholders bring their cherries to a shared washing station.
Only the ripest red cherries are picked. They are pulped, fermented overnight and washed in channels of spring water, then dried on raised beds for two weeks.
We have bought from the same station for three years. We pay before the harvest, so the farmers are not waiting for their money, and every year the coffee tastes a little more like itself.
Jasmine when you open the bag, peach and black tea in the cup. Brew it as filter or pour-over to get the most from it.

latte-art-evenings.title: Latte art evenings, every first Thursday
latte-art-evenings.excerpt: Pour a heart, then a tulip, then a rosetta. Bring a friend; we bring the milk.
content: On the first Thursday of every month we stay open late and hand the steam wand over to you. Our baristas show you how to texture milk and pour a heart, then a tulip, then, if the evening goes well, a rosetta.
Six places, so everyone gets time on the machine
All the milk you can steam and a slice of cake
Ask at the counter or call us on 0117 496 0123. Places go quickly, so book a month ahead if you can.

bread-before-dawn.title: Why the bread is ready before you are
bread-before-dawn.excerpt: The first loaves go in at five. A morning in the room behind the counter.
content: Our baker, Ade, starts at four. By five the first loaves are in the oven and by half past seven, when we open, the shelf behind the counter is full.
A loaf of our country sourdough is mixed the morning before, folded through the day and left to prove slowly in the cold overnight. The long, cool rise is where the flavour comes from.
Croissants and cardamom buns go in after the bread, in the same oven as it cools. The buns are the first thing to sell out, which is why we let you order them ahead.
At closing time, what is left goes to the food bank on Station Road, or becomes tomorrow's bread pudding.

cold-brew-tonight.title: A cold brew you can start tonight
cold-brew-tonight.excerpt: A jar, a sieve and eighteen hours. The easiest coffee you will ever make.
content: Cold brew asks for patience, not skill. Start it tonight and it is ready for tomorrow afternoon.
100 g of coffee, ground coarse like breadcrumbs
A big jar, and a sieve lined with a paper filter
Stir the coffee into the water so every grain is wet.
Cover and leave in the fridge for 18 hours.
Strain through the lined sieve. Twice, for a cleaner cup.
Keep it in the fridge for up to a week. Serve over ice, half and half with water or milk.

yesterdays-sourdough.title: Five things to do with yesterday's sourdough
yesterdays-sourdough.excerpt: A day-old loaf is not a lost loaf. Our favourite ways to use the end of it.
content: A good sourdough is at its best for toast on day two. By day four, it is time to get creative.
Thick toast, butter and our wildflower honey.
Croutons: torn, tossed in olive oil and baked for ten minutes.
Panzanella, with ripe tomatoes and plenty of olive oil.
Breadcrumbs, frozen in a bag for the next time you need them.
Bread pudding, the way we make it at closing time.
Keep the loaf cut side down on a board, or in a cloth bag. Never the fridge: it goes stale faster there than anywhere.
